topics_covered: Leprosy (PB MDT, Type 1 reaction, nerve involvement)
Bullous disorders (Pemphigus vulgaris, Bullous pemphigoid, Dermatitis herpetiformis)
Connective tissue disorders (Dermatomyositis, CREST syndrome, Psoriatic arthritis)
Skin tumors (Melanoma, Marjolin's ulcer, Kaposi's sarcoma)
Drugs (Dapsone, Methotrexate/folic acid, IL-17 inhibitors and IBD)
Basic science (Melanocyte location, Mast cells, Collagen types, HPV risk)

questions.q: A 30-year-old farmer presents with 3 hypopigmented anesthetic patches on the trunk with absent hair growth. Slit skin smear is negative. According to WHO MDT guidelines, the correct treatment regimen is:
opts: Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Dapsone 100mg daily for 6 months
Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Clofazimine 300mg monthly + Dapsone 100mg daily for 12 months
Rifampicin 600mg daily + Dapsone 100mg daily for 6 months
questions.exp: This is paucibacillary (PB) leprosy (2–5 lesions, smear negative). WHO MDT-PB = Rifampicin 600mg once monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100mg daily (self-administered) for 6 months. Option B is the MB leprosy regimen. Dapsone monotherapy is obsolete due to resistance. Daily rifampicin is not the WHO PB regimen.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with patchy alopecia showing broken hair stumps and 'black dots' at follicular orifices on the scalp. KOH examination reveals endothrix invasion (arthrospores inside the hair shaft). The most likely causative organism in the Indian subcontinent is:
questions.exp: Black-dot tinea capitis is caused by endothrix species — arthrospores form inside the hair shaft, causing it to break at scalp level leaving black dots. In India, Trichophyton violaceum is the predominant endothrix species. Trichophyton tonsurans predominates in the Americas. Microsporum canis and M. audouinii cause ectothrix infections with positive Wood's lamp fluorescence.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with vesicular eruption on the right auricle and external ear canal, ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy, and sensorineural hearing loss. This constellation is diagnostic of:
opts: Bell's palsy with secondary otitis externa
Acute mastoiditis with facial nerve compression
questions.exp: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is caused by VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of CN VII. The triad of auricular vesicles + ipsilateral LMN facial palsy + cochleo-vestibular symptoms (hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo) is pathognomonic. Treatment: Acyclovir 800mg 5 times/day + prednisolone for 7-10 days, initiated within 72 hours for best results.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active man presents with a painful, soft ulcer with undermined ragged edges on the glans penis and tender unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain of ulcer discharge shows small gram-negative bacilli arranged in a 'school of fish' pattern. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Features: painful soft ulcer with undermined edges, unilateral tender inguinal bubo, and the 'school of fish'/'railroad track' Gram stain pattern. Contrast with syphilis (painless indurated ulcer) and LGV (painless primary ulcer + groove sign). Treatment: Azithromycin 1g single dose OR Ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters on normal-appearing skin and painful oral erosions for 3 months. Nikolsky sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG and C3 deposition in an intercellular 'fishnet' pattern throughout the epidermis. The primary autoantigen targeted is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (mucosal-dominant type) is caused by IgG autoantibodies against Desmoglein 3. When both skin and mucosa are involved (mucocutaneous type), antibodies against both Dsg1 and Dsg3 are present. Dsg1 alone is targeted in pemphigus foliaceus (superficial blisters, no mucosal involvement). BP180 is targeted in bullous pemphigoid. Collagen VII is in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, raising arms) and a dusky violet periorbital rash with edema. She also has flat-topped violaceous papules over the dorsal knuckles bilaterally. These knuckle papules are called:
questions.exp: Gottron's papules are flat-topped, violaceous papules and plaques over the dorsal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints. They are pathognomonic of dermatomyositis. The heliotrope rash (lilac discoloration of eyelids with periorbital edema) is also characteristic. Adult dermatomyositis requires workup for occult malignancy. Associated antibodies include anti-Jo1, anti-Mi2, anti-MDA5.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman notices a mole on her back that has been changing over 6 months. Dermoscopy shows irregular pigment network, regression structures, and a blue-white veil. Among the ABCDE criteria for melanoma, which single criterion has the highest sensitivity for early detection?
questions.exp: Evolution (change in size, shape, color, or any new symptom such as bleeding or crusting) is the most sensitive single ABCDE criterion for melanoma detection. A previously stable lesion that begins to change should always raise suspicion. Dermoscopic features of blue-white veil (regression + melanin in dermis) and irregular pigment network are highly specific for melanoma.

questions.q: A 35-year-old hairdresser with chronic occupational hand eczema is referred for patch testing to identify contact allergens. According to standard ICDRG guidelines, patch test readings should be performed at:
questions.exp: Standard patch test reading times per ICDRG guidelines are Day 2 (48h) for initial reading when patches are removed, and Day 4 (96h) for final reading to detect late reactions. A Day 7 reading may be added for metals (nickel, gold) and corticosteroids, which can show very late reactions. Reading only at 48h will miss late-positive reactions occurring after patch removal.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman is prescribed dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. She should be screened prior to initiation for a genetic deficiency that predisposes to the most serious acute adverse effect of dapsone, which is:
opts: CYP2D6 deficiency leading to retinal toxicity
G6PD deficiency leading to hemolytic anemia
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia in all patients, but these are markedly exaggerated in G6PD deficiency. G6PD screening before starting dapsone is mandatory. The dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (fever, rash, hepatitis) is HLA-B*13:01 associated (especially in Han Chinese). TPMT deficiency is relevant to azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine toxicity.

questions.q: In normal adult epidermis, melanocytes are predominantly located in the:
opts: Basal layer at the dermoepidermal junction
questions.exp: Melanocytes are dendritic cells of neural crest origin that reside in the basal layer (stratum basale) at the dermoepidermal junction. The melanocyte-to-basal keratinocyte ratio is approximately 1:10. Melanocytes synthesize melanin in melanosomes and transfer them to surrounding keratinocytes via dendritic processes, providing UV protection. Melanocyte density is constant across races; skin color differs due to melanosome size/distribution.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient on MDT for borderline tuberculoid leprosy suddenly develops acute erythema and edema of pre-existing skin lesions with severe neuritis causing footdrop. Slit skin smear remains negative. This reaction is best classified as:
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction occurs in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL) due to a delayed-type hypersensitivity upgrade. Features: acute inflammation of EXISTING lesions and acute neuritis (cardinal feature). MDT must be CONTINUED; steroids (prednisolone 40-60mg/day tapered over 3-6 months) are added. ENL (Type 2) occurs in BL/LL leprosy with systemic features and new erythematous tender nodules.

questions.q: A 2-month-old infant presents with white plaques on the buccal mucosa and tongue that can be scraped off leaving a raw erythematous base. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast. The first-line treatment is:
opts: Nystatin oral suspension 100,000 units/mL, 1mL in each cheek QID
questions.exp: Oral candidiasis (thrush) in infants is treated with nystatin oral suspension 100,000 units/mL applied in each cheek 4 times daily for 7-14 days. Nystatin is poorly absorbed from GI tract, making it safe and effective locally. Fluconazole is reserved for refractory cases or immunocompromised infants. Griseofulvin is only active against dermatophytes. Terbinafine is not approved for oral candidiasis.

questions.q: A 5-year-old immunocompetent child presents with multiple discrete, pearly, skin-colored papules with central umbilication on the trunk and axillae. The causative virus belongs to the family:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a Poxvirus (genus Molluscipoxvirus). MCV types 1-4 exist; MCV-1 is most common in children (skin-to-skin contact), MCV-2 in sexually active adults. The central umbilication contains molluscum bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies on histology — large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions). In immunocompetent children it is self-limiting over 6-12 months.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a small self-healed painless genital papule 3 weeks ago, followed by progressive unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Enlarged nodes above and below the inguinal ligament create a pathognomonic 'groove sign.' The causative organism is:
opts: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by C. trachomatis serovars L1, L2 (most common), and L3. The groove sign (Greenblatt sign) — inguinal nodes split by the inguinal ligament into two groups — is pathognomonic. LGV complement fixation titer >1:64 confirms diagnosis. Treatment: Doxycycline 100mg BD for 21 days. Non-LGV serovars (A-K) cause trachoma and urogenital chlamydiosis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with intensely pruritic papulovesicles symmetrically distributed over the extensor elbows, knees, and buttocks. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae. This condition is strongly associated with:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is pathognomically characterized by granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips on DIF. It is almost universally associated with celiac disease. Anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) antibodies cross-react with epidermal transglutaminase. Gluten-free diet is the cornerstone of treatment for both skin lesions and enteropathy. Dapsone provides rapid relief of itch.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, calcinosis cutis on the fingers, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias on the face. She reports heartburn and difficulty swallowing solids. The autoantibody most specific for this form of systemic sclerosis is:
questions.exp: This is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), formerly CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is found in ~70-80% of lcSSc and is highly specific. The major complication is pulmonary arterial hypertension. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc (risk of pulmonary fibrosis). Anti-dsDNA and Anti-Sm indicate SLE.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man with a 15-year-old venous stasis ulcer on the medial malleolus develops a rapidly growing, exophytic, fungating mass within the ulcer. Biopsy reveals well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. This malignant transformation of a chronic wound is termed:
questions.exp: Marjolin's ulcer is an SCC (occasionally BCC or melanoma) arising in chronic scars, ulcers, burn wounds, sinus tracts, or osteomyelitis. It characteristically lacks pain (destroyed nerve supply) and tends to have a delayed regional lymph node spread initially, but is biologically aggressive. The latency period from injury to malignancy can be 20-40 years. Wide surgical excision is the treatment of choice.

questions.q: On dermoscopy of a seborrheic keratosis, the most characteristic and specific features are:
questions.exp: Dermoscopy of seborrheic keratosis (SK) shows: milia-like cysts (white round structures), comedo-like openings/crypts (dark follicular plugs), cerebriform/gyrate pattern, and sharp demarcation ('stuck-on' appearance). Arborizing vessels and leaf-like areas are features of BCC. Blue-white veil suggests melanoma. The combination of milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings is highly diagnostic of SK.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient with psoriasis on methotrexate 15mg/week complains of oral ulcers and nausea. These mucocutaneous and GI side effects can be significantly reduced by co-administering:
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting folate stores. Oral ulcers (mucositis), nausea, and fatigue are common adverse effects. Folic acid supplementation 1-5mg/day (given on days not taking MTX) significantly reduces these side effects without compromising anti-psoriatic efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used for MTX toxicity rescue/overdose. B12 does not mitigate MTX side effects.

questions.q: In IgE-mediated (Type I) immediate hypersensitivity reactions in the skin such as urticaria and angioedema, the principal effector cell responsible for degranulation and release of histamine is:
questions.exp: Mast cells are the central effector cells in Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity. They bear high-affinity IgE receptors (FcεRI). Cross-linking of surface-bound IgE by antigen triggers degranulation releasing preformed mediators (histamine, tryptase, heparin) and newly synthesized lipid mediators (PGD2, LTC4/D4/E4) and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-4). Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting cells involved in Type IV (delayed) reactions.

questions.q: A 35-year-old leprosy patient develops gradual clawing of the 4th and 5th fingers of the right hand. The peripheral nerve most commonly affected in leprosy causing this deformity is the:
opts: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
questions.exp: The ulnar nerve is the most commonly affected nerve in leprosy, palpable and thickened behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow. Ulnar nerve paralysis causes clawing of the 4th and 5th fingers (loss of interossei and hypothenar muscles), hypothenar wasting, and loss of little finger abduction. Order of nerve frequency in leprosy: ulnar > common peroneal > posterior tibial > median > radial > facial > great auricular.

questions.q: A 50-year-old diabetic man presents with thickened, yellow-brown, brittle toenails with distal subungual hyperkeratosis affecting 3 toenails. KOH mount of nail clippings shows branching septate hyphae. The most effective oral treatment for dermatophyte onychomycosis of the toenails is:
questions.exp: Terbinafine (allylamine) is the treatment of choice for dermatophyte onychomycosis with the highest mycological cure rates (~75-80% for toenails). Dose: 250mg/day for 6 weeks (fingernails) and 12 weeks (toenails). It accumulates in the nail plate via the nail bed and persists for months. Nystatin has NO activity against dermatophytes. Griseofulvin has lower cure rates. Fluconazole 150mg weekly for 6-9 months is an alternative but inferior.

questions.q: A 23-year-old woman presents with multiple soft, cauliflower-like verrucous growths on the vulva. HPV genotyping identifies types 6 and 11. Regarding the oncogenic potential of these HPV subtypes:
opts: High risk: similar malignant potential to HPV 16 and 18
Low risk: cause benign condylomata acuminata with minimal malignant potential
Intermediate risk: approximately 15% lifetime risk of SCC
questions.exp: HPV types 6 and 11 are low-risk (non-oncogenic) subtypes causing benign condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts). Malignant transformation is rare. High-risk oncogenic types include HPV 16, 18, 31, 33, 45 — responsible for cervical SCC, vulvar SCC, and penile SCC. Bowenoid papulosis (high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia with benign behavior) is associated with HPV 16. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is caused by HPV 6 and 11.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with a painless, beefy-red, granulomatous ulcer with raised rolled edges on the genitalia that bleeds on contact. Tissue crush smear shows Donovan bodies (intracytoplasmic inclusions within large macrophages). The first-line treatment per CDC guidelines is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units IM single dose
Azithromycin 1g orally once weekly for minimum 3 weeks until complete healing
questions.exp: Granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions in macrophages seen on Giemsa/Wright/Leishman stain. CDC-recommended treatment: Azithromycin 1g weekly OR 500mg/day for minimum 3 weeks AND until lesions completely heal. Alternatives include doxycycline 100mg BD for ≥3 weeks (not 7 days — insufficient). Benzathine penicillin is for syphilis.

questions.q: A 72-year-old man presents with multiple tense blisters on an urticarial base on the flexural areas and trunk. Oral mucosa is spared. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone. The primary autoantigen is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is caused by IgG autoantibodies targeting BP180 (NC16A domain) and BP230. BP180 (collagen XVII) is the primary pathogenic antigen — its NC16A domain is the immunodominant epitope. Key differences from pemphigus: tense blisters (subepidermal split), negative Nikolsky sign, linear DIF, mucosa usually spared. Collagen VII is targeted in EBA and dystrophic EB. Laminin-332 in mucous membrane pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man with longstanding psoriasis develops asymmetric oligoarthritis with prominent DIP joint swelling and nail dystrophy. Rheumatoid factor is negative. The nail finding most characteristic of psoriatic arthritis is:
opts: Oil-drop sign (salmon patch under nail) with pitting
questions.exp: The oil-drop sign (salmon patch) — a translucent yellow-red discoloration under the nail plate resembling a drop of oil — is highly characteristic of psoriatic arthritis. Nail pitting (>20 pits) also supports the diagnosis. The combination of DIP arthritis, dactylitis ('sausage digit'), nail oil-drop sign, and psoriatic skin lesions is diagnostic of psoriatic arthritis. CASPAR criteria include nail lesions as a diagnostic component.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 count of 85 cells/μL presents with multiple violaceous non-tender plaques on the lower extremities and hard palate. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular channels and extravasated red blood cells. The herpesvirus causally associated with this neoplasm is:
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also called Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV). HHV-8 infection is necessary but not sufficient — immunosuppression is the key co-factor. AIDS-related KS presents with violaceous lesions on skin, oral mucosa, GI tract, and lungs. HAART with immune reconstitution can cause regression. Liposomal doxorubicin is used for systemic disease.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient with extensive vitiligo (>30% BSA) unresponsive to topical therapies is prescribed PUVA therapy. The psoralen most widely used for both oral and topical PUVA worldwide is:
questions.exp: 8-methoxypsoralen (8-MOP, methoxsalen) is the most widely used psoralen worldwide for both oral PUVA (0.4-0.6mg/kg taken 1.5-2h before UVA) and topical PUVA (0.001-0.1% solution). 5-MOP is preferred in some European centers due to fewer GI side effects. TMP (trioxsalen) is used for topical/bath PUVA with lower phototoxicity. Angelicin (monofunctional psoralen) has lower efficacy. Contraindications to PUVA: pregnancy, photodermatoses, previous arsenic exposure, SLE.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and concurrent active Crohn's disease requires biologic therapy. Which biologic agent should be AVOIDED due to risk of worsening inflammatory bowel disease?
questions.exp: IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) and IL-17RA inhibitors (brodalumab) are associated with new-onset or worsening of IBD (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis). IL-17 plays a protective role in gut mucosal immunity; its inhibition disrupts barrier function. These agents are contraindicated in active IBD. Anti-TNF agents (infliximab, adalimumab) and IL-23 inhibitors (ustekinumab, risankizumab, guselkumab) are effective for BOTH psoriasis and IBD.

questions.q: A medical student is reviewing dermal histology and asks about the predominant collagen type in adult skin dermis. The correct answer is:
opts: Type I collagen (~80% of dermal collagen, thick bundles in reticular dermis)
Type IV collagen (basement membrane lamina densa)
Type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils at dermoepidermal junction)
questions.exp: Type I collagen is the predominant collagen in adult skin dermis, comprising ~80-85% of total dermal collagen forming large bundles in the reticular dermis. Type III collagen (~15%, reticulin fibers) is more abundant in fetal skin and papillary dermis. Type IV collagen forms the basement membrane zone (lamina densa). Type VII collagen forms anchoring fibrils — deficient in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (dominant: COL7A1 dominant-negative mutation; recessive: loss-of-function mutation).
